http://www.bgnes.com/health/transylvania.text: “They call this place the Bermuda Triangle of Transylvania,” tour guide Marius Lazin says as he takes me on a nighttime walk through the Hoia-Baciu Forest near the Romanian city of Cluj-Napoca. The forest, which stretches across about one square mile, is considered one of the most haunted places in the world, The Guardian reports. Legends of unusual phenomena date back centuries. According to one of them, a local shepherd disappeared along with 200 sheep. Hoia-Baciu gained international fame in 1968, when military technician Emil Barnea photographed an object that he described as a UFO above a circular clearing in the center of the forest. Since then, the site has attracted yogis, shamans, ufologists and paranormal researchers. The forest, however, is facing another, far more real threat. The western suburbs of Cluj-Napoca, which has become a technology hub with more than 400,000 residents, are gradually expanding, while property developers are pushing for permission to clear parts of the forest to build residential buildings. The Hoia-Baciu Project, co-founded by Lazin, is trying to draw attention to the natural and tourism value of the area. Among the most widespread stories are accounts of people disappearing without a trace, strange rashes, phones and cameras suddenly switching off, as well as sensations of being touched or pushed by an invisible force. One of the best-known legends tells of a five-year-old girl who disappeared during a family picnic and reappeared five years later with no memory of what had happened and without having aged. Lazin shows Barnea’s photographs and other images depicting what are said to be flying saucers, glowing orbs and strange silhouettes. Although such photographs do not constitute reliable evidence of paranormal phenomena, Barnea’s case is unusual - he had no financial interest in publishing them and even lost his job in the military because of them. The trees in the forest are particularly striking, with trunks twisted and bent into unusual shapes. Various explanations have been offered for this - from strong winds to naturally high levels of radiation in the soil - but scientific studies have not established a convincing cause. At the center of the forest is a perfectly circular clearing where Barnea took his famous UFO photographs. Lazin gives visitors a device for measuring electromagnetic fields, but when they attempt to detect unusual activity, it turns out that the readings were caused by an incoming message on a phone. After several hours in the forest, nothing appears that can be described as supernatural. Nevertheless, the strange trees and unusual clearing leave enough room for the imagination. Transylvania has long been associated with legends and dark stories - from beliefs in strigoi, the dead who return, to the legendary Count Dracula. Hoia-Baciu, however, remains one of the places where the boundary between reality and imagination seems particularly thin. | BGNES

https://www.dw.com/en/can-germany-defend.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IlIk One defense method involves interceptor drones, which chase drones and capture them with a net Image: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement On August 25, German media reported on a third drone allegedly found near Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. A drone and a substance — which initial assessments suggest could be around 50 grams of Hexogen, a highly explosive military-grade explosive — were reportedly discovered in a field outside the airport grounds. Consequently, public broadcasters NDR and WDR, and the daily broadsheet Süddeutsche Zeitung are speculating about a plot that may be far more extensive than what has been publicly disclosed so far. Speaking on the sidelines of a federal government retreat in the state of Brandenburg, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) stated: "Germany has increasingly come into the crosshairs of hybrid attackers." Merz also pointed to measures aimed at better protecting the public. Just a few days ago, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) inaugurated a drone security research center in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, not far from Leipzig and Halle in Saxony. How could drones laden with explosives fly unhindered near or into Leipzig/Halle airport and remain unnoticed for at least several hours? Interior Minister Dobrindt had immediately spoken of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers." Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because one drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation. However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights . Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, security expert Nico Lange warned. "We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW. Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense. "That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident. The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible. Why coordinating Germany's drone defense is difficult Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions. In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted. Drones move quickly, and any response must be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off somewhere in the country, it's initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. Only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility are the federal police allowed to step in. Europe's defense: Latest drone technology shown in Berlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Will Germany's federal police lead on drone defense? Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities. "The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer. Many, including the Greens, suggest the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. The federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense in December, and Dobrindt now wants to expand the unit following the incident at Leipzig airport. Originally, 130 staff positions across four locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across eight locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry. Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany? As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to deploy the Bundeswehr , Germany's armed forces, to take care of drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that police are responsible for upholding security in the country. A Defense Ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing," is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he added. In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster." German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Why German airports and train stations still lack protection There is also a lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment used to defend against drones. "There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. "So far, they have not intercepted a single drone, and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place." The German Police Union (GdP) has also lamented the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke. An Interior Ministry spokesperson said large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The eight large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle," she said. The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of the year. This article was originally written in German. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: The Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, Canada Photograph: Google Maps View image in fullscreen The Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, Canada Photograph: Google Maps Canada Man and police officer wounded in exchange of gunfire near Ontario synagogue Officials say man was critically injured and officer was wounded in Yom Kippur incident near Belleville synagogue Associated Press Mon 21 Sep 2026 10.56 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire on Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition. The Canadian province’s special investigations unit said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, about 110 miles (160km) east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer encountered the man at about 7.10pm and that both were taken to a hospital. Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated. The special investigations unit, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene. Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was under way. Doug Ford, Ontario’s premier, said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur. “I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur,” Ford said in a post on social media. Ford said Jewish people “have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear” and called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted. “My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones,” Ford said. York regional police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship. Sunday’s shooting comes months after Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, warned that the country was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism. Carney cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues, and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel. Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings. Image: Harald Tittel/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement A fighter jet crashed near the US air base in Spangdahlem, Germany , on Tuesday. The plane crash occurred at approximately 2:30 p.m. local time (12:30 UTC). The cause of the incident is currently under investigation. The US military confirmed that the plane was an F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing and that its pilot was able to safely eject from the aircraft. "The pilot ejected safely and is receiving medical care," the base said in a statement. At least one person was injured, authorities said Image: Harald Tittel/dpa/picture alliance Local authorities in the remote Eifel region also confirmed that one person had been injured. "Following a plane crash in the vicinity of US Air Base Spangdahlem, fire and emergency response teams from the Eifel District of Bitburg-Prüm were dispatched to the scene," the district said on its website. "No comments can be made on the further details of the event from the side of the Eifel district at this time." A NATO operations center Spangdahlem Air Base is a NATO operations center that was built in the early 1950s. The US Air Force's 52nd Fighter Wing is garrisoned there. The base is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron comprising around 20 aircraft. It is located north of the city of Trier in Rhineland-Palatinate , not far west of the border to Luxembourg. The facility at Spangdahlem is considered one of the most important airfields for the US military in Germany, alongside Ramstein base, outside the city of Kaiserslautern. Some 5,000 US military and civilian personnel-plus dependents are stationed at Spangdahlem, with around 700 to 800 Germans also employed at the facility. Photograph: Jess Hurd/PA View image in fullscreen Olivia Grange, Jamaica’s minister of culture, has hailed the King’s decision to refer her slavery reparations petition to the privy council. Photograph: Jess Hurd/PA Jamaica Jamaica hails King’s decision to refer slavery reparations petition to privy council as ‘really big deal’ The move comes after Jamaica’s culture minister Olivia Grange travelled to the UK earlier this month to lodge the historic petition Natricia Duncan Caribbean correspondent Tue 22 Sep 2026 21.15 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 22.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google King Charles has referred a landmark slavery reparations petition from Jamaica to a high-level UK appeals court for legal advice, Jamaica’s culture minister announced in parliament on Tuesday. Referring to the move as a “really big deal”, Olivia Grange told Jamaica’s MPs the monarch had confirmed that their legal questions have been passed on to the London-based privy council – the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries. The petition seeks guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences. Jamaica’s plea to the king: use your authority to ensure colonial slavery is examined | Olivia Grange Read more “Indeed we went fearless and boldly into this chapter when we petitioned the king on Monday, September 7, 2026 – one day after the 245th anniversary of the commemoration of the Zong massacre, an event that captures the barbarity of chattel enslavement,” Grange said in parliament. “The king could have ignored us. The king could have delayed responding to us. The king could have made a decision not to refer the questions to the privy council, or he could make a decision to refer the questions,” she said, before adding “King Charles has referred the petition filed on the 7th of September, 2026, on behalf of the people of Jamaica to the Judicial Committee of the privy council.” Jamaica had activated a rarely used mechanism in the Judicial Committee Act 1833 , which allows the king to refer questions of “legal or constitutional nature” to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts, according to the country’s legal counsels. The minister said that taking the matter to the International Court of Justice, was not an option for Jamaica. “The United Kingdom has placed specific reservations on the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ which prevent the Court from adjudicating on disputes between the United Kingdom and the government of any other country which is or has been a Member of the Commonwealth”. A privy council opinion would not compel the UK government to pay reparations, but Jamaican officials believe it could shape negotiations and legal options and set a precedent for other Commonwealth nations seeking reparations. Earlier this month, Grange led a Jamaican delegation to London to officially lodge the petition . While in the UK, the group, lawyers and members of the country’s national council on reparation met diaspora communities, MPs, church leaders and cultural institutions – among them the British Museum, from which Jamaica is seeking the return of artefacts taken during colonial rule. Tuesday’s announcement follows the Caricom Regional Conference on Reparations , which took place in Barbados last week. Officials at the conference said that Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal. Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options. Speaking at the conference, Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today. He said: “When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?” Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”. Grange told parliament that the country is “awaiting directions from the Judicial Committee of the privy council as to the next steps to be taken in the case. And the attorney general is preparing to deal with the case”.
